about: CAE (Computer Aided Engineering), FH Technikum Wien master's programme, 2nd semester, after the slides of Krach: 02_FEM-Einfuehrung_2020.pdf (Krach 2020a), 03_FEM-Entwicklungsprozess_Nichtlinear_Statik-Dynamik_2018.pdf (Krach 2018), 04_FEM-LowEnd-HighEnd_Integration_Extrapolation_2021.pdf (Krach 2021) and 05_FEM_Materialeigenschaften_2020.pdf (Krach 2020c), and the solved ModSim tasks VO-Aufgaben-mit-Lösungen.pdf (Puhwein 2020). Pages are the PDF pages, read in the text layer and, for equations set as pictures, from the page images on 2 Nov 2026. The slides print few numbers (σ = 60 MPa on 02 p. 40, the 8- and 64-fold cost of 02 p. 54, the sketch of 04 p. 62); the rest of the questions were worked by hand from the slides' equations and say so. tests/unit/labs-data.test.js recomputes every answer with the core and fails if they disagree.

lectures.title: Linear or nonlinear, static or dynamic

labs.title: Springs as finite elements
labs.idea: Two nodes held by three springs: write each node's force balance and the system becomes [K]{u} = {f}, the basic equation of the finite element method. Each spring adds its own small matrix to [K].

equations.note: The force balance of each node

equations.tex: \begin{bmatrix} k_1 + k_{12} & -k_{12} \\ -k_{12} & k_2 + k_{12} \end{bmatrix} \begin{Bmatrix} u_1 \\ u_2 \end{Bmatrix} = \begin{Bmatrix} f_1 \\ f_2 \end{Bmatrix}
equations.note: The same in matrix form: the stiffness matrix
Basic equation of the FEM; Ku = F for statics
One spring's element matrix, added into [K] at its two nodes

practice.question: k1 = k12 = k2 = 1000 N/mm, f1 = 100 N, f2 = 0. How far does node 1 move, in µm?
practice.source: Worked by hand from 02 FEM-Einführung, p. 30

practice.question: Same springs and forces: how far does node 2 move, in µm?
practice.source: Worked by hand from 02 FEM-Einführung, p. 30
practice.solution: u2 = 1000·100/3·10⁶ = 0.0333 mm = 33.3 µm: node 2 follows through the joining spring.

labs.title: Discretising a circle
labs.idea: Approximate a circle's perimeter by n chords, one finite element each: the result is the sum of the element lengths, always too short, and the error falls as the elements multiply.

equations.note: The perimeter as the sum of the elements, each between nodes i and j
One chord of n equal chords in a circle of diameter d
The area of the polygon, for the circle's area of p. 48

practice.question: A circle of d = 100 mm by 6 equal elements: what perimeter does the polygon give?
practice.source: Worked by hand from 02 FEM-Einführung, p. 49
practice.solution: Each chord is 100·sin 30° = 50 mm; 6·50 = 300 mm, against π·100 = 314.2 mm.

practice.question: With 12 elements, how many per cent short of π·d is the polygon?
practice.source: Worked by hand from 02 FEM-Einführung, p. 49
practice.solution: 12·sin 15° = 3.1058 against π = 3.1416: 1.14 % short, about a quarter of the 4.5 % of 6 elements.

labs.title: A bar and mesh refinement
labs.idea: A bar held at one end, loaded at its tip and along its length, in n linear elements. The nodes come out exact; each element's stress is constant, so the peak at the support is missed until the elements are small. Finer meshes cost more.
labs.law: σ = F/A,  ε = u/L,  k = EA/L

equations.note: Stress, internal resistance per area; strain, deformation per length

equations.eq: E = σ/ε in the linear elastic range
equations.note: The modulus is the slope of the stress–strain diagram; steel 210 000, aluminium 70 000 N/mm²

equations.eq: k = EA/h for one element of length h
equations.note: From F = k·u with the two lines above

equations.eq: u(x) = [F·x + q(Lx − x²/2)]/(EA),  σ(x) = [F + q(L − x)]/A
equations.tex: u(x) = \frac{F x + q\,(L x - x^2/2)}{EA},\quad \sigma(x) = \frac{F + q\,(L - x)}{A}
equations.note: The exact solution for an end force F and a line load q
Cost of refinement in a solid mesh: quadratic in the degrees of freedom

practice.question: A steel bar, L = 1000 mm, A = 100 mm², E = 210 000 MPa, with 1000 N at its tip. How far does the tip move, in µm?
practice.source: Worked by hand from 03 Nichtlinear, p. 30 and 05 Materialeigenschaften, p. 9
practice.solution: u = F·L/(EA) = 1000·1000/(210 000·100) = 0.0476 mm = 47.6 µm. One element gives it exactly.

practice.question: The same bar with a line load q = 2 N/mm and no tip force, in 4 elements. What stress does the first element report?
practice.source: Worked by hand: exact σ(0) = qL/A = 20 MPa
practice.solution: The first element spans 0–250 mm and carries the mean of its stress: q·(L − h/2)/A = 2·875/100 = 17.5 MPa, 12.5 % below the 20 MPa at the support.

practice.question: Halving the element length of a solid mesh multiplies the elements by 8. By what factor does the solving time grow?
practice.source: Krach (2020a), 02 FEM-Einführung, p. 54, printed: 64
practice.solution: Time grows with the square of the degrees of freedom: 8² = 64.

labs.lecture: Krach (2020a), 02 FEM-Einführung, pp. 19 and 52–55; Krach (2018), p. 30

labs.title: The cantilever: by hand and by elements
labs.idea: The course's bending beam, 10 × 10 mm, 100 mm long, 100 N at the tip: σ = M/W = 60 MPa and u = F·l³/(3EIy) by hand. Beam elements reproduce both exactly; under a line load the moment inside each element is only approximate.

equations.note: The bending stress at the clamp of the course's example
The cantilever's tip deflection, a classic hand formula
Second moment and section modulus of a rectangle; W as on p. 40

equations.eq: u = q·l⁴/(8EIy),  M(x) = F(l − x) + q(l − x)²/2
equations.tex: u = \frac{q l^4}{8 E I_y},\quad M(x) = F(l - x) + \frac{q (l - x)^2}{2}
equations.note: The line load's tip deflection and the moment along the beam
The beam element with cubic shape functions: deflection and slope at each node

equations.tex: w(x) = \frac{F x^2 (3l - x)}{6 E I_y} + \frac{q x^2 (6l^2 - 4lx + x^2)}{24 E I_y}
equations.note: The exact deflection curve the chart plots; at x = l it gives the two tip formulas above

practice.question: The course's beam: 10 × 10 mm, 100 mm long, 100 N at the tip. What is the bending stress at the clamp?
practice.source: Krach (2020a), 02 FEM-Einführung, p. 40, printed: 60 MPa

practice.question: The same beam in aluminium, E = 70 000 MPa. How far does the tip move?
practice.source: Worked by hand from 03 Nichtlinear, p. 20, with E of 02 FEM-Einführung, p. 14

practice.question: The beam with a line load of 1 N/mm and no tip force, in 2 beam elements: what moment does the first element give at the clamp, in N·mm? (Exact: 5000 N·mm.)
practice.source: Worked by hand from the exact nodal deflection and slope at x = 50 mm
practice.solution: The nodes are exact: w(50) = 4 427 083/EI, θ(50) = 145 833/EI. The element's curvature at x = 0 gives M = 6/50²·4 427 083 − 2/50·145 833 = 10 625 − 5 833 = 4 792 N·mm, 4.2 % low.

labs.lecture: Krach (2020a), 02 FEM-Einführung, pp. 14 and 40–47; Krach (2018), p. 20

labs.title: Shape functions
labs.idea: Inside an element the displacement is built from shape functions, one per node: 1 at its own node, 0 at the others, all summing to 1. Linear elements draw straight lines between nodes, quadratic ones parabolas through a mid-node.

equations.eq: Ni = 1 at node i, 0 at the others; Σ Ni = 1
equations.note: The properties of shape functions: defined on the whole element, equal on shared edges
Linear, two nodes at ξ = 0 and 1 (drawn on p. 56)
Quadratic, nodes at ξ = 0, ½ and 1 (drawn on p. 56)
The displacement method: shape functions first, then strains, then stresses

practice.question: A quadratic element: what is the mid-node's shape function at ξ = 0.25?
practice.source: Worked by hand from 04 Integration–Extrapolation, pp. 55–56
practice.solution: Nm = −4·0.25·(0.25 − 1) = 0.75; the two end functions take the remaining 0.25 between them.

practice.question: y = x² on 0–1 by one linear element: what does the element give at x = 0.5? (The curve has 0.25.)
practice.source: Worked by hand from 04 Integration–Extrapolation, p. 56
practice.solution: The nodes hold 0 and 1; halfway, N1 = N2 = ½, so ½·0 + ½·1 = 0.5. A quadratic element would give 0.25 exactly.

labs.title: Integration points and extrapolation
labs.idea: Elements compute their stresses at integration (Gauss) points. Plots show nodal values: extrapolated from the points, then averaged across neighbouring elements. Near steep gradients the extrapolation overshoots.
labs.law: σ_node = extrapolated from the integration points, averaged over the elements at the node

equations.note: The averaged nodal value from N adjacent elements
The two Gauss points of a linear element in natural coordinates
Straight-line extrapolation from the two points to the element's nodes

practice.question: A linear element has 100 MPa and 150 MPa at its two integration points. What does extrapolation give at the node beyond 150?
practice.source: Worked by hand; the sketch of 04 Integration–Extrapolation, p. 62 reads about 170
practice.solution: Mean 125 MPa, half-difference 25 MPa; the node at ξ = 1 lies √3 times as far out as the point at 1/√3: 125 + 1.732·25 = 168.3 MPa.

practice.question: Same element: what is the node beyond 100 MPa?
practice.source: Worked by hand; the sketch of 04 Integration–Extrapolation, p. 62 reads 80

labs.title: A nonlinear spring and Newton's iteration
labs.idea: A linear model answers in one solve. When stiffness changes with the displacement (material, geometry, contact), an implicit solver iterates: follow the tangent, check the residual, repeat, in load steps.
labs.law: KT(ui)·Δu = P − F(ui),  ui+1 = ui + Δu
labs.lawTex: K_T(u_i)\,\Delta u = P - F(u_i),\quad u_{i+1} = u_i + \Delta u

equations.note: The linear structural behaviour; nonlinear when material, geometry or contact change
A spring that stiffens (c > 0) or softens (c < 0), standing for any nonlinearity
The tangent stiffness
Newton–Raphson: one linear solve per iteration

practice.question: k = 100 N/mm, c = 10 N/mm³, P = 500 N, one load step from u = 0. Where does the first Newton iteration land?
practice.source: Worked by hand from the definition
practice.solution: KT(0) = 100 N/mm and the residual is 500 N: Δu = 5 mm, the linear answer. F(5) = 500 + 1250 = 1750 N overshoots, so the next iteration steps back.

practice.question: Same spring and load: what displacement does the iteration converge to?
practice.source: Worked by hand: 100·u + 10·u³ = 500

labs.lecture: Krach (2018), 03 Nichtlinear, Statik–Dynamik, pp. 26–35; Krach (2020a), 02 FEM-Einführung, pp. 58–59

labs.title: Natural frequencies and mode shapes
labs.idea: Without load and damping, [M]{ẍ} + [K]{x} = 0: mass and stiffness alone set the natural frequencies. Each degree of freedom has one frequency and one mode shape, a shape without size.

equations.note: The dynamic equation; Mü + Cu̇ + Ku = F(t)
No damping, no load: the equation of eigen analysis
One mass on one spring

equations.tex: M = \begin{bmatrix} m_1 & 0 \\ 0 & m_2 \end{bmatrix},\quad K = \begin{bmatrix} k_1 + k_2 & -k_2 \\ -k_2 & k_2 \end{bmatrix}
equations.note: The two-mass oscillator (dampers left out)
The eigenvalues are the squared natural angular frequencies; the eigenvectors the mode shapes

practice.question: One mass of 1 kg on a spring of 100 N/m: what is its natural frequency?
practice.source: Worked by hand from 03 Nichtlinear, p. 44 and ModSim VO-Aufgaben, p. 8

practice.question: The two-mass oscillator with m1 = m2 = 1 kg and k1 = k2 = 100 N/m: what is the higher natural frequency?
practice.source: Worked by hand from ModSim VO-Aufgaben, p. 28

labs.lecture: Krach (2018), 03 Nichtlinear, Statik–Dynamik, pp. 39–47; Puhwein (2020), ModSim VO-Aufgaben, pp. 27–28

labs.title: Explicit or implicit time steps
labs.idea: A transient analysis steps the equation of motion through time. An explicit solver only evaluates and is cheap per step, but its step must stay below a limit; an implicit solver solves an equation each step and stays stable at any step.
labs.lawTex: M\ddot u + K u = F(t),\qquad \Delta t_\text{explicit} < \frac{2}{\omega}

equations.tex: M\ddot u + C\dot u + K u = F(t)
equations.note: The equation of motion of elastodynamics

equations.eq: Implicit: invert the stiffness matrix; explicit: many time increments
equations.note: The two kinds of solver
The explicit central difference for one mass
The central difference's stability limit

equations.tex: \left(1 + \tfrac{\Delta t^2 \omega^2}{4}\right) u_{n+1} = u_n + \Delta t\, v_n + \tfrac{\Delta t^2}{4} a_n
equations.note: The implicit average-acceleration rule (Newmark, γ = ½, β = ¼), one equation per step
The exact answer the chart plots: the mass released from u0 at rest

practice.question: A mass of 1 kg on 400 N/m: what is the largest stable step of the central difference, in ms?
practice.source: Worked by hand: Δt = 2/ω

practice.question: A stiffer element: 1 kg on 4·10⁶ N/m. How many explicit steps does 50 ms of simulated time need at least?
practice.source: Worked by hand: Δt = 2/ω
practice.solution: ω = 2000 s⁻¹, Δt = 1 ms; 50 ms/1 ms = 50 steps. Stiffer or lighter elements, as in a finer mesh, shrink the step.

labs.lecture: Krach (2020a), 02 FEM-Einführung, pp. 23 and 27; Krach (2018), 03 Nichtlinear, Statik–Dynamik, pp. 38 and 45
